name: bluewater-26-kongo
lines: There was a company that stayed in business for one thousand four hundred years.
It outlived the samurai. It outlived two world wars.
And then, in about twenty years, it was gone.
Its name was Kongo Gumi. It built temples.
Here is how it lasted. And the one mistake that ended it.
Japan. The year five hundred and seventy eight.
A prince wants a great Buddhist temple.
Nobody in Japan knows how to build one.
So he sends across the sea, to Korea, for master carpenters.
One of them is named Shigemitsu Kongo.
He builds the temple. In the city we now call Osaka.
And when it is done, he does not go home. He stays. And starts a business.
That is the whole business. Build temples. Repair temples.
Rule one. Do one thing. And be the best at it.
For the next fourteen centuries, his family does exactly that.
Wars. Fires. Crashes. Governments that rise and fall. They keep building.
A scroll three metres long lists the heads of the family. Forty generations.
So how does a family business survive forty handovers?
Most do not survive two.
Here is their secret. The job did not always go to the oldest son.
It went to the one who was best at the work.
If no son was good enough, a skilled son in law took the family name. And took over.
The thirty eighth head of the company was a woman.
Rule two. The best person runs it. Not the next in line.
Fourteen hundred years. One family. One craft.
Then come the nineteen eighties.
Japan is booming. Land prices climb and climb.
Everyone is borrowing money to buy property. It looks like the easiest money in the world.
And the temple builders decide to join in.
They borrow heavily. And they invest in real estate.
It has nothing to do with temples.
Then the bubble bursts.
The land is worth far less than they paid. The debt is exactly what they borrowed.
They keep building temples. Temples are still most of their sales.
But the craft cannot earn fast enough to carry the debt.
By two thousand and six, the debt was reported at three hundred and forty three million dollars.
And after one thousand four hundred and twenty eight years, the family firm is taken over by a bigger builder.
Rule three. What ends you is rarely the work. It is the thing you did on the side.
The carpenters still build temples today. Under the same name. But the family no longer owns it.
Fourteen centuries of doing one thing well. Undone by twenty years of doing something else.
So here are the three. One. Pick the thing you are best at. And stay with it.
Two. Give the work to whoever does it best.
And three. When easy money shows up, outside what you know, that is the dangerous day.
Stay in your craft. It is what your customers came for.
Your business. Our marketing department. Bluewater Co.
